st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source is broadly compatible with retaining human judgment as models improve, but it does not substantively address the cluster’s central concerns about bounded-task evidence, verification, workflow complements or apprenticeship risk. Instead, it shifts attention toward predicted GPT-5 improvement, commercial adoption and the intersection of AI with unlicensed-practice regulation.
qs: IAALS has this new report on the regulation of legal services—the unlicensed practice of law statutes and how they intersect with AI—is worth spending a little time on.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: McCormack shifts the focus from organisational adoption, incentives and workflow redesign to public use outside traditional legal services and the need to reconsider legal regulation. Her argument constructively prioritises regulatory reform and access-to-justice realities rather than the cluster’s principal organisational-change framing.
qs: So whatever the gray area is, I don't think there are many people who are going to slow down and say, "Gosh, I can't afford a lawyer, but I'm not going to go get an answer from GPT-5 (which I can now do on a free version), even though that might help me a lot in figuring out how to navigate this problem.” It’s just not going to work that way.
So it makes sense for us to at least start having a conversation about whether some of our regulatory architecture is anachronistic.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports continued human verification and supervised AI use, but it does not address the cluster’s principal claim that automation is eroding the junior-work apprenticeship through which lawyers acquire the expertise needed to verify outputs. Its recommendations on experimentation and shared learning fall short of endorsing the proposed reconstruction of associate training.
qs: And as you said, all of the ethical obligations to check the outputs over and over again, to not rely on anything that comes out of it—to treat it and supervise it as you would an inexperienced lawyer—remain.
All the things that you and I advocate and teach remain the same: experiment; share with your colleagues and others what you're learning, where the limitations are, where the benefits could be.

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The excerpt only previews discussion of GPT-5 and an IAALS report and notes growing personal AI use. It does not address AI-assisted versus autonomous adjudication, dispute-resolution redesign, legitimacy, safeguards, access, or performance evidence, so no position on the cluster proposition can be determined.
qs: And we are here today on release week for the newest model from OpenAI, GPT-5, and we're going to talk all about that today in our What Just Happened segment (where we try to connect for our legal audience what is happening in the broader landscape) before we dive into our main topic this week, where we will talk about a report from the Institute for the Advancement of the American Legal System (or IAALS, for short).

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value

qs: You still need an actual three-dimensional human to help you through the system, which to me feels like a whole different problem to solve (one that could have a more seamless solution if we had more of a tech/API integration approach here).

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

kp.k: Judge hallucinations should be contextualized against tolerated human error
kp.d: McCormack supports withdrawing hallucination-containing judicial opinions and providing courts with training and resources, but argues that criticism should compare AI errors with existing judicial error rather than an error-free baseline. Using GPT-5 to crunch data, she reports last year's Sixth Circuit reversal rate as about 5.6% averaged across criminal and civil cases, with civil cases at 10%, and Michigan Court of Appeals reversals at 21%, plus 11% receiving partial relief. These are her reported AI-assisted calculations, not an independently established comparison of human and AI accuracy. She describes reversal rates as an incomplete floor because of harmless error, subsequent exonerations and cases never appealed.
qs: But as somebody who practiced in courts for a long time and worked in courts for a long time, the human error that we tolerate is so significant.

So that number, by the way—the Sixth Circuit last year, the reversal rate was about 5.6% (if you average the criminal and civil cases; the civil ones were actually 10%). The Michigan Court of Appeals: 21% of cases were reversed, and 11% gave partial relief.
So this floor—this rate of error that we tolerate—is a very squishy, soft floor.

kp.k: Human thinking and verification remain essential around AI assistance
kp.d: The discussion frames current AI assistance as useful in the middle of work rather than as an end-to-end replacement: humans must initially frame and organize problems and finally verify outputs. Leonard describes abandoning AI-assisted workshopping to develop her own ideas, and argues that offloading work can undermine learning when developing knowledge and connections is the goal. McCormack qualifies the continued need for front-end human thinking as a present judgment, explicitly leaving its status five years ahead uncertain.
qs: You really are still valuable at the front and the back.

The back we know (check your cites before you file the brief, or check your cites before you deliver the opinion). But the front is also critical—just in framing and organizing and thinking about what it is that you're then going to get the middle-to-middle help with.
Maybe it won't be true five years from now (I have no idea), but it definitely feels true now.
But if you're working on a project where your goal really is to learn about the content and develop new ideas and new connections, you want your brain to be deeply invested in that learning process.

kp.k: GPT-5 automates model selection but disrupts established workflows
kp.d: During GPT-5 release week, McCormack describes automatic routing between faster and deeper-thinking models as reducing users' need to select the appropriate model manually. She reports that extending GPT-5 to free users while removing older models triggered backlash, including practical problems for people who had built GPTs around previous models. She says she believes paid access to 4.0 was subsequently restored, and suggests advance transition notice could have helped users manage compatibility problems.
qs: What it does is, you put in a query and it decides which model it needs to answer it.
Even free users got GPT-5. The other models disappeared, so you no longer had access to 4.0 or o3 or whatever model you were using and liked before.
Some of it is more practical: I know people who built specific GPTs on those previous models, and when there's a new model, they don't always work right.

kp.k: Reported benchmark gains do not establish direct human superiority
kp.d: McCormack reports that Vals places GPT-5 above Gemini 2.5 Pro and xAI's latest model on legal benchmarks, and describes more robust legal work in her own informal comparisons. Leonard cites GPT-5 accuracy of 84.6% on the Vals leaderboard and human lawyers at around 70% on a variety of tests in March. Crucially, she says task definitions and comparability need further examination; the transcript does not establish a like-for-like human-versus-model finding. Expectations that models will continue improving are the speakers' predictions.
qs: On the benchmarks—on the legal benchmarks, the Vals study has GPT-5 now as the top model, coming in just above Gemini 2.5 Pro which is just above xAI’s latest model.
We have those slides that we use in presentations of the Vals benchmarking of human lawyers from back in March, putting human lawyers on a variety of tests at around 70% accuracy.

A quick look at the Vals benchmarking accuracy puts GPT-5 at 84.6% on that leaderboard. I'd want to dig into the data and see exactly what the tasks are and how that compares with those earlier lawyer benchmarks.

kp.k: Improved models do not remove lawyers' verification obligations
kp.d: Both speakers maintain that GPT-5's reported improvements leave lawyers' safeguards and ethical responsibilities unchanged. McCormack analogizes its work to that of a strong summer or new associate whose output still requires checking before filing. Leonard recommends experimentation and sharing benefits and limitations rather than making constant model tracking the priority for most lawyers. This is an augmentation-and-supervision model, not permission to rely directly on AI output.
qs: But it's not good enough to trust without checking.
So I think you can think of it as a great first start, but I still think lawyers need all the same safeguards that they needed with the previous models.

And as you said, all of the ethical obligations to check the outputs over and over again, to not rely on anything that comes out of it—to treat it and supervise it as you would an inexperienced lawyer—remain.

kp.k: Consumer-centered regulation could expand access to civil legal help
kp.d: Leonard presents the IAALS report as shifting regulation from lawyer-centered protection toward consumer needs, endorsing AI's potential to help individuals and small businesses who cannot afford legal assistance. She reports case studies of Courtroom5, ZAF Legal, Roxanne and Rentervention, and AI-powered court chatbots in Nevada and Arizona. These are examples of applications and an argument for access expansion, not quantified evidence of improved outcomes. She says the report addresses hallucinations, bias and privacy alongside the opportunity. McCormack discloses membership of IAALS's advisory board.
qs: What I really appreciate about IAALS' approach is that it is trying to move us from a more lawyer-centric approach to a more consumer-facing approach to regulation.
Most Americans and small businesses can't afford legal help.
So the report digs into some tools that are already doing just that, like Courtroom5, ZAF Legal, Roxanne, and Rentervention, and it gives some nice use cases and case studies.
It addresses all of the risks that lawyers are well aware of—the things that we're concerned about: hallucinations, biases, privacy concerns, those kinds of things.

kp.k: Public AI exposure outpaces evidence about legal usage
kp.d: Leonard acknowledges the absence of strong data on ChatGPT use for legal help, while arguing that people searching Google for legal assistance already encounter AI summaries. Reporting Margaret Hagan's research presented at the IAALS gathering, she says affiliation with major technology companies increases AI trust, but people prefer human legal support for sensitive matters such as domestic violence, divorce and criminal issues. The report consequently raises questions about public education, partnerships and collecting usage data; no sample size or quantified trust findings are supplied.
qs: we don't yet have great data on ChatGPT usage for legal help

And the report points to some research that Margaret Hagan from Stanford presented during the gathering, showing that trust in AI is growing because of its affiliation with big tech companies—especially Google (since the public trusts Google and internet searches generally).

But it also showed that people trust human legal support over AI (or technology generally), especially for more sensitive matters like domestic violence proceedings or divorce, (in family law contexts, criminal law contexts—things that have real human stakes).

kp.k: IAALS recommends soft measures before possible formal regulation
kp.d: In Leonard's account, the report proposes two phases rather than immediate comprehensive regulation. Phase one combines best-practice guidance, monitored sandboxes, consumer-outcome data, technology-company partnerships and enforcement discretion or safe harbors. Only after further learning would possible formal measures include UPL and ethics-rule changes, certification, risk-tiered regulation and interstate uniformity. Leonard separately identifies her concern about protecting lawyers rather than consumers as editorial commentary, not simply the report's conclusion.
qs: Phase one it describes as "soft power" actions.

Those actions include issuing best-practice guidelines for developers, deployers, courts, and consumers; launching regulatory sandboxes so we can test tools in a safe and monitored environment (which several states—Arizona, Minnesota, and some others—have already done); collecting more robust data on consumer outcomes; exploring partnerships with big tech companies to improve legal AI; and using prosecutorial discretion and safe harbor policies to give innovators breathing room.

Some of that formal regulation could include adjusting unauthorized practice of law (UPL) and ethics rules if needed, creating certification systems for AI legal tools, developing a risk-based regulatory framework (with different rules for high-risk cases versus low-risk cases), and pursuing uniformity across states.

kp.k: Fragmented UPL rules complicate regulation of boundaryless technology
kp.d: Leonard argues that jurisdiction-specific UPL frameworks fit poorly with rapidly changing technology that crosses borders. McCormack expects people unable to afford lawyers to use freely accessible AI regardless of regulatory ambiguity, supporting reconsideration of existing architecture. She also identifies an unresolved institutional issue: legislative repeal of a UPL statute might not free innovators from constraints because courts retain inherent authority over legal practice. Her Pennsylvania example is hypothetical, not a reported repeal or legal determination.
qs: One issue the report talks about—and that I also think is very problematic—is that there are so many different jurisdictions and so many different UPL rules and frameworks, while technology is boundaryless and constantly changing.
And it feels obviously timely—people are using the technology whether the law allows them to or not.
Maybe, but maybe not—because the court ultimately has inherent power to regulate the so-called practice of law, even in the absence of a statute. So it's still a gray area that needs discussion.

kp.k: Community justice workers signal broader professional-boundary reform
kp.d: McCormack reports growing authorization for nonlawyer community justice workers to provide limited information, advice and help where consumers lack lawyers, citing a recent D.C. development and describing the total as reaching double digits. She also reports support from the Conference of Chief Justices and an ABA resolution passed, in her account, the previous day encouraging state programs. She connects these developments with an emerging institutional willingness to rethink regulation, while describing an NCSC–Thomson Reuters Institute UPL-and-AI paper as forthcoming within weeks and disclosing her advisory role.
qs: A number of state supreme courts recently have piled on to what seems to be a growing trend of allowing community justice workers—people other than lawyers—to provide some legal information, advice, and help in certain kinds of cases where the consumer is not going to have access to lawyers.
D.C. did it recently, bringing the number of states that have done that into double digits.

And I think just yesterday, at the ABA annual meeting, the ABA passed a resolution encouraging states to create community justice worker programs (which really means encouraging state supreme courts, since state supreme courts are the ones that regulate the practice of law).

kp.k: Court workflows limit AI's end-to-end access-to-justice potential
kp.d: Leonard predicts increasingly capable AI research, next-step guidance and drafting, but identifies a remaining gap between those outputs and carrying out procedural actions. Recalling a conversation with Garfield Law's UK founders, she contrasts their court API connection with what she describes as a physically routed domestic system. She proposes community justice workers, paraprofessionals and better technical integration as possible bridges, while maintaining that humans would still be needed.
qs: But then there's the gap between that and the actual activity that needs to take place. And it seems like that's where the gap will remain.
I assume that's where these community justice workers and various paraprofessional roles (different from lawyers) come into play.

You still need an actual three-dimensional human to help you through the system, which to me feels like a whole different problem to solve (one that could have a more seamless solution if we had more of a tech/API integration approach here).

kp.k: New supervised service models could extend beyond licensed lawyers
kp.d: McCormack speculates about a new legal technology justice supervisor role, associated training and a scalable business model outside the traditional law firm, potentially sold by subscription to community organizations. Such workers could help consumers formulate useful legal questions and act on outputs. She contrasts her own legally informed model testing with the difficulty an untrained user might have asking the right questions, arguing that necessary front- and back-end human assistance need not always come from licensed lawyers. These are proposed roles and business possibilities, not demonstrated operating models.
qs: I've been trying to think of what a legal tech justice supervisor could be. I'm trying to envision whole new categories of legal workers, what it would take to train them, and then how to scale a business model that has nothing to do with the traditional law firm model.
You could imagine different community organizations thinking, "Yeah, we'll take a subscription to your legal justice supervisor program."
So I still think there's a front-end and a back-end role for humans. It's just not clear to me why those humans necessarily need to be licensed lawyers for all issues and for all people, right?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The speakers describe stronger but still supervised legal AI, expanding consumer self-help, and possible new regulatory and service-delivery models rather than fully autonomous legal services.
pts.d:
1. Bridget McCormack says GPT-5 produces more robust legal work and better reasoning than earlier models, but remains a first draft requiring lawyer verification. Jen Leonard agrees that the upgrade does not change lawyers' ethical obligations to supervise and check outputs. Leonard also predicts continuing improvements in model reliability.
2. McCormack describes AI's present role as 'middle to middle': humans must frame and organize work before using AI and check it afterward. Leonard says using AI too early can obstruct the thinking needed to learn, develop ideas, and produce quality writing; she sees greater value in later refinement.
3. McCormack reports using GPT-5 to assemble and analyze judicial-error statistics and produce slides, talking points, and written explanations. Her accompanying argument is that AI errors should be considered against existing human error in courts, rather than an assumed error-free baseline. She does not establish that AI makes fewer errors than courts.
4. Leonard says AI offers an unprecedented opportunity for individuals and small businesses unable to afford lawyers to obtain help. She describes existing consumer tools and court chatbots. She infers that people already encounter legal AI through Google summaries; McCormack argues that people will seek free AI help regardless of regulatory uncertainty.
5. Leonard's account of the IAALS report attributes to that report a consumer-centered, two-phase regulatory approach: first guidelines, monitored experimentation, outcome data, partnerships, and enforcement flexibility; then possible formal regulation, including UPL and ethics changes, certification, risk differentiation, and interstate uniformity. Both speakers support reconsidering existing regulatory arrangements. McCormack cautions that repealing a UPL statute might not remove courts' inherent regulatory authority.
6. Leonard predicts an increasingly capable AI research-and-drafting stage but a persistent gap between advice and taking action in court. She suggests community justice workers and paraprofessionals could bridge that gap, and that better court technology integration could make workflows more seamless without eliminating humans.
7. McCormack proposes, speculatively, new legal-worker categories such as a 'legal tech justice supervisor' and subscription services for community organizations outside the traditional law-firm model. She argues that front-end framing and back-end assistance need not always be supplied by licensed lawyers.
8. McCormack says changing underlying models can disrupt custom GPTs built on previous versions. Leonard reports that some legal-domain tools have already adopted GPT-5, transmitting model improvements through existing legal software.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Support consists of reported Vals benchmarking, personal experiments and work experience, an IAALS report and its examples, and institutional developments; several future service models remain explicitly speculative.
pts.d:
1. McCormack cites Vals AI's legal benchmarking as ranking GPT-5 just above Gemini 2.5 Pro and xAI's latest model, and her own repeated legal questions across GPT-5, Gemini, and Claude during the preceding week. Leonard reports GPT-5 accuracy of 84.6% and approximately 70% for human lawyers in earlier March benchmarking, but expressly says she needs to inspect the tasks and comparability. The transcript therefore offers these figures without establishing a like-for-like human/model comparison. Broader claims about reasoning, coding, and reduced sycophancy include release claims and personal impressions rather than a separately presented study.
2. The human-framing argument rests on the speakers' experiences of AI-assisted writing and planning. Leonard refers generally to research on learning and AI, but provides no study design or quantified finding.
3. McCormack reports AI-calculated appellate figures: about 5.6% Sixth Circuit reversals in the previous year when averaging criminal and civil cases, 10% for civil cases, and Michigan Court of Appeals figures of 21% reversed and 11% receiving partial relief. She supplies neither underlying datasets nor independent verification in the transcript. She treats these as an incomplete and contestable starting point, proposing additions for harmless error, exonerations, and unappealed cases. Two unnamed judges' recently withdrawn opinions containing hallucinations prompted the exercise; these incidents are not model error-rate measurements.
4. Leonard cites the IAALS report's examples of Courtroom5, ZAF Legal, Roxanne, Rentervention, and AI-powered chatbots in Nevada and Arizona. She acknowledges limited data on ChatGPT use for legal help. Her account of Margaret Hagan's presented research attributes to that research growing trust in AI through major technology brands, alongside a preference for human legal support in sensitive matters; no methods or figures are supplied.
5. The regulatory proposals are attributed to the IAALS report, not presented as demonstrated effects. McCormack points to community justice worker authorizations, support from the Conference of Chief Justices, an ABA resolution, and a forthcoming National Center for State Courts/Thomson Reuters Institute paper as signs of institutional momentum. She discloses her IAALS advisory-board membership and her advisory and access-to-justice roles in the latter project.
6. Leonard draws on a prior conversation with the UK Garfield Law founders about court API connectivity. The transcript offers no comparative workflow study.
7. McCormack's proposed supervisor roles and subscription model are thought experiments, not evaluated businesses or measured access-to-justice outcomes.
8. McCormack refers to people she knows whose custom GPTs do not always work properly after a model change. Leonard cites social-media posts about legal-tool upgrades and OpenAI's release announcement identifying legal as a use case.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The discussion takes place during GPT-5 release week in 2025; current improvements are qualified by mandatory human checking, while regulatory reforms and new delivery models are conditional and undated.
pts.d:
1. The GPT-5 assessments concern release week and experiments during the preceding week. Leonard expects models to become more capable and reliable over time but supplies no dated target. Neither speaker treats the reported benchmark ranking as permission to rely on unchecked legal output.
2. McCormack explicitly limits her human-front-and-back framing to present experience and says she does not know whether it will remain true five years later. Leonard's caution about early AI use particularly concerns projects whose purpose is learning and developing original connections, rather than every use of AI.
3. McCormack's judicial-error project is ongoing: the appellate figures are available, while harmless-error analysis is still being developed and other categories are proposed. Her Sixth Circuit figures refer to 'last year,' relative to the 2025 episode. The two judicial hallucination incidents occurred in the preceding few weeks.
4. Consumer exposure and some self-help tools are described as already present. Broader access gains are opportunities rather than measured outcomes, particularly for those without affordable lawyers. McCormack's expectation that consumers will proceed despite regulatory uncertainty is a behavioral prediction, not a reported usage survey.
5. IAALS phase one precedes any decision on phase-two formal regulation; formal rules would follow learning and data collection and are proposed only if needed. No implementation deadline is given. The contemplated Pennsylvania repeal is hypothetical, qualified by possible continuing judicial authority. The related NCSC/TRI paper is expected within a few weeks.
6. Leonard expects research and next-step assistance to improve 'increasingly,' but gives no date for resolving court-workflow gaps. More seamless delivery depends on technology integration and available human assistance.
7. McCormack's new-role model depends on designing training, finding organizations willing to hire or subscribe, and potentially combining community justice worker programs with changes to technology regulation and UPL. She expresses possibility rather than certainty.
8. The model migration effects are immediate release-period observations; reports of access restoration are qualified by McCormack's 'I think' and concern paid users.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are practicing lawyers, judges, underserved individuals and small businesses, nonlawyer legal workers, consumer-tool developers, and institutions regulating or operating courts.
pts.d:
Lawyers and law firms: Better general-purpose and legal-domain AI can support research, drafting, reasoning, and refinement, while lawyers retain responsibility for framing tasks and verifying output. Custom-tool users may face disruption from underlying model changes. The speakers do not quantify employment, revenue, staffing, or billing effects.
Judges and courts: AI creates both assistance opportunities and risks from fabricated material in opinions. McCormack advocates resources and training and a comparison with existing human error. Court technology and filing processes constrain how far AI advice can translate into completed legal action.
Individuals and small businesses unable to afford lawyers: The predicted benefit is access to self-help information, research, drafting, and procedural guidance. These are access-to-justice claims, not enterprise legal-budget savings. Consumers may still need help identifying legally relevant facts, asking questions, and navigating courts.
People in sensitive disputes: Leonard's account of the research highlights continued preference for human support in domestic violence, divorce, family, and criminal matters. The report's proposed risk-based approach would distinguish higher- and lower-risk uses.
Community justice workers and paraprofessionals: The speakers envisage expanded front-end and back-end assistance roles alongside AI. McCormack questions whether licensed lawyers must supply those functions for all issues and all users, rather than proposing universal replacement of lawyers.
Community organizations and prospective service providers: They could potentially hire or subscribe to trained legal-technology assistance services outside traditional law firms. This is a proposed delivery model, not an identified established ALSP.
Developers, deployers, technology companies, courts, bar associations, legislatures, and state supreme courts: The proposed regulatory sequence would give them roles in guidelines, experimentation, outcome monitoring, partnerships, certification, and possible UPL reform. Fragmented jurisdictional rules create a challenge for rapidly changing technology that crosses state boundaries.
